                             4. Conclusions

                           The main goal of this project was to design a face detection and identification system
                           capable of autonomously creating and utilizing a reference image database. This objective
                      was successfully achieved, as the system demonstrated solid performance throughout
                                 testing. Built on a Raspberry Pi microcomputer, the application operates efficiently, achiev-
                           ing an average recognition time of 10.5 s. When standardized procedures for capturing
                             reference and test images are followed under controlled environmental conditions, the
                         system delivers near-flawless accuracy, as confirmed by the test results. Although the

Appl. Sci. 2025, 15, 887                                                                                                         24 of 27



                          system performs well for small user groups and controlled scenarios, there are several areas
                        where further research is needed to improve its robustness and scalability:

                                        -    Database Size and Biometric Variations: To assess scalability and reliability, the system
                             needs to be tested with larger databases, exceeding a thousand users, including
                                 individuals with significant biometric similarities.
                                        -   Hardware Impact: The current setup uses a standard Raspberry Pi-compatible camera
                             module. Initial tests suggest that higher-resolution cameras could improve accuracy
                           and facial feature detection, particularly when the reference images are of higher
                                  quality than the test images. Exploring the impact of hardware upgrades on system
                                performance, especially under challenging conditions like poor lighting or occlusions,
                           would be a valuable next step.
                                        -   Algorithm and Library Performance: The system employs the Haar cascade classifier
                                   for face detection and data matrix generation, achieving high accuracy with frontal
                                     faces. However, its performance decreases with extreme facial angles. Leveraging
                                  additional tools from the OpenCV library, such as deep learning-based models, could
                                  mitigate these limitations and broaden the system’s capabilities.
                                        -    Security Enhancements: While the system works well for access control in environ-
                             ments dealing with sensitive data, it is vulnerable to spoofing via printed photographs.
                           Adding features like thermal imaging to differentiate living faces from static images
                                or incorporating additional biometric verifications (e.g., fingerprint or retina scans)
                           would enhance security.

                            Beyond access control, the system’s flexibility enables a range of potential applications:

                                        -    Retail and Surveillance: tracking customer movements or behavior in stores.
                                        -   Data Collection: gathering pedestrian statistics or analyzing consumer habits.
                                        -   Media Analysis: measuring screen time for actors in media productions.

                             Although these extensions were beyond the original scope of the project, they highlight
                            the system’s adaptability for future development [69,70]. Implementing such features
                      would require additional modules, like object tracking, and further refinement of the
                            algorithms. This system has proven to be a reliable facial recognition tool under specific
                            conditions [71]. While it may not be suited for high-security environments requiring
                           zero errors, it provides a strong foundation for further innovation in facial recognition
                          technology [72]. With the proposed improvements and adaptations, the system has the
                             potential to be expanded into a variety of use cases, ranging from access control to data
                              analytics and surveillance.

Article
The Application of Adaptive Tolerance and Serialized Facial
Feature Extraction to Automatic Attendance Systems

Chun-Ling Lin *  and Yi-Huai Huang



                               Department of Electrical Engineering, Ming Chi University of Technology, No. 84, Taishan Dist.,
                       New Taipei City 243, Taiwan; m07128014@mail2.mcut.edu.tw
                                     * Correspondence: ginnylin@mail.mcut.edu.tw; Tel.: +886-2-2908-9899 (ext. 4819)


                                Abstract: The aim of this study was to develop a real-time automatic attendance system (AAS) based
                         on Internet of Things (IoT) technology and facial recognition. A Raspberry Pi camera built into a
                            Raspberry Pi 3B is used to transfer facial images to a cloud server. Face detection and recognition
                                     libraries are implemented on this cloud server, which thus can handle all the processes involved with
                               the automatic recording of student attendance. In addition, this study proposes the application of
                              data serialization processing and adaptive tolerance vis-à-vis Euclidean distance. The facial features
                             encountered are processed using data serialization before they are saved in the SQLite database;
                            such serialized data can easily be written and then read back from the database. When examining
                               the differences between the facial features already stored in the SQLite databases and any new
                                     facial features, the proposed adaptive tolerance system can improve the performance of the facial
                                recognition method applying Euclidean distance. The results of this study show that the proposed
                     AAS can recognize multiple faces and so record attendance automatically. The AAS proposed in this
                             study can assist in the detection of students who attempt to skip classes without the knowledge of
                                   their teachers. The problem of students being unintentionally marked present, though absent, and
                                the problem of proxies is also resolved.

                          has been subject to sustained development over the past 30 years. It has great potential for
                          use across numerous government and commercial applications [10–12]. Security cameras
                          with facial recognition capabilities are presently common in airports, ofﬁces, universities,
                 ATM installations, banks, and indeed, in any location with a security system [13–15].
                        Parmar and Mehta described the most common methods of face recognition, such as
                            the holistic matching method, the feature extraction method, and hybrid methods; and
                         proposed a number of face recognition applications, such as face identiﬁcation, access
                               control, and security and identity veriﬁcation [13]. Khandelwal et al. suggested various
                              face recognition processing methods and adopted a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)
                              to develop a face recognition algorithm [14]. Norouzi explored face recognition based on
                         deep neural networks and described various facial expression recognition applications [15],
                          such as student attendance systems and building security systems.
                      Among all the techniques applied to AAS, facial recognition is considered to be the
                        most efﬁcient [16]. Although facial recognition based on deep learning techniques [17–19]
                          has high accuracy, the model is complex and the recognition speed is slow, even when
                        working on just a single image. In order to realize real-time facial recognition of stu-
                              dents, two particular computer vision libraries—the open-source computer vision libraries
                        (OpenCV) [20,21] and Dlib [22–24]—have been applied in many previous studies. Kar et al.
                         adopted the OpenCV and Light Tool Kit (FLTK) to develop an AAS system and suggested
                              that OpenCV can provide a simple-to-use computer vision infrastructure that can help
                           people build fairly sophisticated vision applications quickly. The OpenCV library contains
                           over 500 functions that span many areas of vision [20]. Joseph et al. adopted face detection,
                          128-dimension face encoding extraction, and support-vector machine (SVM) training to
                          develop a system [21]. Boyko et al., explored the features and analyzed the pros and cons of
                     OpenCV and Dlib [22]. Xu et al., adopted Dlib to detect faces, and then adopted CNN and
                           a deep residual network (ResNet) for real-time face recognition [23]. Ambre et al. explored
                          a real-time face recognition system using easily attainable components and libraries, such
                            as Raspberry PI; Dlib, a Face Recognition library; and OpenCV [24].
                                 This has been done on the basis that the utilization of libraries allows easy application
                        and reimplementation. The OpenCV library is a cross-platform computer library which can
                          provide an infrastructure for computer vision applications and allow the use of machine
                           perception easily within commercial products. However, OpenCV [25] suffers from the
                         problems of missed detections, false detections, and in effect poor recognition overall.
                   On the other hand, Dlib is a cutting-edge toolbox which includes various different AI
                               tools and which allows the creation of complex software programs for solving real-world
                         problems [26]. Dlib can deal with bad and inconsistent lighting and various facial po-
                               sitions (such as tilted or rotated).  It also achieves high performance within real-world
                          implementations both in terms of speed and accuracy [27]; all this makes it suitable as a
                             basis from which to develop an AAS. The challenges of AAS include how to make the
                           attendance registration and management systems efﬁcient, time-saving, simple, and easy.
                           Furthermore, an AAS needs to recognize, accurately, multiple faces, faces in inconsistent
                              lighting conditions, and faces presented via various positions. Pandey et al. combined
                             the on-demand resource availability of cloud computing, which can store and retrieve the
                           captured video anytime. Additionally, its surveillance mechanism involves the Viola–Jones
                           algorithm for face detection by analyzing captured data [28]. Shanthi and Svalakshmi de-
                          veloped a surveillance method by using a face recognition based unmanned aerial vehicle
                       (UAV) [29]. The method of UAV was implemented on Raspberry Pi module with Python
                                libraries which included OpenCV, Dlib, Face_recognition, and Numpy. Gupta and Singh
                         used in-memory computation to develop a real-time face recognition system. Even while
                            the number of faces is increasing, it can still keep the frame rate steady during the entire
                            process [30]. These recent studies developed an AAS system based on Raspberry Pi, a cloud
                         computing environment, and face detection algorithms. They can make the systems simply,
                                  easily, and more efﬁciently.

Electronics 2022, 11, 2278                                                                                                        3 of 15



                           The aim of this study was to develop a real-time AAS system based on Internet
                             of Things (IoT) technology and facial recognition, which can handle the registration of
                             students. The main contributions of this study are threefold:

                                   1.   Building a cloud server to develop face detection and recognition algorithms. A
                              Raspberry Pi Camera system built into a Raspberry Pi 3B was used to capture and
                                     transfer images to a cloud server with a high-speed GPU. The development of our face
                                  detection and recognition algorithms was based on this cloud server, which handles
                                 the processes involved in registering student attendance, namely, comparing faces
                               using extracted features stored in a database.
                                   2.   Creating an SQLite database to save students’ facial features based on data serializa-
                                       tion, which we propose as the strategy for this process. In order to create the SQLite
                                 database, the students’ facial features will be put through data serialization before
                                they are saved using SQLite.
                                   3.   Improving the performance of face recognition using adaptive tolerance with respect
                                   to Euclidean distance. In comparing the facial features found in the database with
                                 the new facial features encountered in the input, the former needs to be subjected
                                   to data deserialization. The proposed adaptive tolerance method can improve the
                              performance of the facial recognition processes using Euclidean distance.

                             With the implementation of our proposed AAS, students cannot skip classes without
                            the knowledge of their teachers.
                               This study is organized as follows. In Section 2, the proposed AAS schematic and
                       methods are described. Section 3 shows the results of this study. Section 4 discusses the
                         proposed AAS system and indicates the advantages of the proposed methods. Section 5
                           provides concluding remarks.

                                   2. Methods

                               Figure 1 shows the schematic of our proposed AAS. The design of our AAS system
                            includes four main components: a Raspberry Pi camera built into a Raspberry Pi 3B; a
                         Django background processing system, the OpenCV image processing library, and the Dlib
                             face detection and face recognition module. For each student, the proposed AAS system
                        must save a headshot, and a complete set of facial features derived from this, onto the cloud
                                server. The dimensions of the headshot are reduced to a standard size and then converted
                              to a grayscale image, using OpenCV. Once this is done, the facial landmarks are identiﬁed
                          using the Dlib library. Each set of facial landmarks derived from the students’ faces is
                         saved in SQLite [31] and associated with an appropriate students’ names. A Raspberry
                             Pi camera built into a Raspberry Pi 3B was set up in the classroom in order to capture the
                         images and transfer them to a cloud server through the RESTful application programming
                              interface (API). When the cloud server receives an image, the facial landmarks from this
                          can be extracted using the Dlib library. The newly extracted features can then be compared
                          with those already stored in the SQLite database in order to conﬁrm (or not) the identity of
                            the student. If this identity veriﬁcation is successful, the student is recognized and so the
                              student’s name will show on a computer screen in the classroom as having been marked as
                              in attendance.

                                   2.1. The Cloud Server

                           The Django cloud server has an automatic background task management interface
                       and can provide technical support systems, including a user authentication mechanism;
                                          it (the server) is used to receive the facial images, store these in the database, and process
                       them [32]. This study adopted the Django system as the basis for implementing Raspberry
                             Pi as a web server [33], applying the RESTful API [34]. The latter is an architectural style
                       API that uses HTTP requests to access and use data. Into the Django system, we imported
                            the OpenCV and Dlib libraries. These support the engine in processing the images and so
                             detecting and recognizing the faces of the students.

                                   2.2. SQLite Databases

                           The ﬂowchart in Figure 2 shows how the student database is created via SQLite.
                          SQLite is a popular database management system [35]. In this case, the SQLite database
                              will contain information regarding the students to be detected and recognized. Each
                             student, on enrolment, must provide a headshot which presents a complete set of facial
                                features, as shown in Figure 3a. The convolutional neural network’s (CNN) features, used
                           within the context of the Maximum-Margin Object Detector (MMOD) (MMOD-CNN) face
                             detector in the Dlib library (Dlib CNN), are adopted as the basis by which the faces and
                                their positions within the object are detected, identiﬁed, and recognized [36–38]. The face
                           within the object is extracted from the original headshot and converted to grayscale using
                    OpenCV (Figure 3b). For the Dlib facial recognition network, the image being processed
                        must be transformed into an output feature vector with 128 numerical facial features. These
                             are used to characterize each face [39], as shown in Figure 4.
                                   In order to store, in SQLite, the output feature vectors, each representing the 128 numerical
                              features which in turn represent a particular face, the feature vector needs to be subjected
                              to data serialization. This technique converts data objects represented as complex data
                             structures into a byte stream for storage, transfer, and distribution purposes on physical
                             devices, using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON library) [40]. The name of the subject
                       and the 128 numerical facial features, after JSON serialization, will be stored in the SQLite
                             database, as shown in Figure 5.

                                   2.3. Face Recognition

                                Figure 6 shows the ﬂowchart of the face recognition process proposed and described
                            as follows:

                                   1.   The real-time continuous face recognition AAS, which captures the attendance and
                                 duration of attendance of students from the Raspberry Pi camera set-up, requires that
                              Raspberry Pi Model B.
                                   2.   The raspberry Pi model extracts an image from every six frames of the live video (of
                                 the classroom) and uploads them to the cloud server.
                                   3.   The MMOD-CNN process has been adopted as the process by which the faces—and
                                     their positions within the object—are detected. The object is a list of rectangular
                                      objects. If the MMOD-CNN cannot obtain rectangle objects, we go back to Step 2.
                                   4.  OpenCV crops the image of each face with the object and converts it to grayscale
                                form.
                                   5.   The estimated 128 facial landmarks are obtained using the Dlib facial recognition
                               network.
                                   6.   For facial similarity calculation, the estimated facial landmarks are compared with
                                 the facial landmarks currently stored in the SQLite database. This comparison is
                             performed after the JSON deserialization process has been applied to the existing

                                   2.3.1. Maximum-Margin Object Detector Convolutional Neural Network (MMOD-CNN)

                          a classic histogram of oriented gradient (HOG) features, in conjunction with the linear
                               classiﬁer SVM, pyramid images, and a sliding window detection scheme; the other is based
                       on the Maximum-Margin Object Detector convolutional neural network (MMOD-CNN),
                          a face detector that uses deep learning face detection. The MMOD-CNN can be adopted
                          using cnn_face_detection.py; the function returns a list of rectangle objects which extract
                            the face within the object.

                                   3. Results

                                 In this study, we developed a real-time AAS based on Internet of Things (IoT) tech-
                         nology and facial recognition. A Raspberry Pi 3B setup including a Raspberry Pi camera
                            captures and then transfers six frames from each local video of a face to the cloud server.
                       The development of the facial detection and recognition algorithms is based on the facil-
                                    ities available on the cloud server. In addition, in this study, we propose two strategies
                              in particular: data serialization for storing facial features in SQLite easily and adaptive
                             tolerance (with respect to the width of the facial image) for improving the performance of
                                 facial recognition using Euclidean distance.

                                   3.1. The Performance of Adaptive Tolerance

                                This study proposes adaptive tolerance for improving the performance of face recog-
                              nition using Euclidean distance. The tolerance for face recognition is not ﬁxed, instead
                             of Equation (2). In order to compare the performance of face recognition using ﬁxed
                             tolerance (Figure 7b) with adaptive tolerance (Figure 8), two different tolerances were

                               set in the face recognition using Euclidean distance. The student stood at the same loca-
                              tion (Figures 7b and 8). If adaptive tolerance was adopted to set the tolerance in the face
                             recognition using Euclidean distance, the student could be recognized.





                              Figure 8. Adaptive tolerance for Euclidean distance in the facial recognition task.

                                   3.2. The Performance of Face Detection Using the Dlib CNN and Dlib HOG Libraries

                            The Dlib library is arguably one of the most widely utilized packages for the purposes
                              of facial recognition. This study compares the performance of face detection achieved by
                            Dlib CNN with that achieved by Dlib HOG [42] in Figure 9.

                                   angles, in various lighting conditions, and withocclusions.

                                     efﬁcient.

                           performance, in terms of detecting faces, than Dlib HOG. Hence, this study adopted the Dlib
                 CNN library for the purpose of detecting faces and the positions of faces within frames.

                                   3.4. The AAS System

                                 In order to test the performance of our AAS system (Figure 1), we set it up in the
                               laboratory. The Raspberry Pi camera built into the Raspberry Pi 3B was thus able to capture
                              relevant images, as shown in Figure 11. The Raspberry Pi transferred the images to the cloud
                            server using an appropriate API. The results of the face detection and facial recognition
                            processes are shown in Figure 9a. The face detection and facial recognition system imple-
                       mented in the cloud server using the OpenCV and Dlib libraries successfully supported
                             the automatic registration of the attendance of the students in the cloud server (Figure 12);
                            the results were returned to the Raspberry Pi and shown on the computer screen.

                                 In addition, the AAS system was set up in the laboratory (Figure 11) and actually
                       worked for one minute. The Raspberry Pi Model B sets 12 frames per second for the
                          video stream, and extracts an image from every six frames of the live video. The AAS
                         can work and record the attendance of the students every 0.5 s. Over the 120 occasions
                              of four students’ attendance the recording, the proposed system obtained 100% accuracy;
                                           i.e., four students could be detected and recognized in each image. When the AAS system
                         with face detection using Dlib HOG and the adaptive tolerance for face recognition was
                            involved, only one student could be recognized each time. When the AAS system with
                            the face detection using Dlib CNN and with the ﬁxed tolerance for face recognition was
                            used, only three students could be recognized each time. The last student could be detected
                          but not recognized. Thus, the results show that the proposed system is better than the
                   AAS system at face detection using Dlib HOG, and the AAS system with face detection
                           using Dlib CNN and a ﬁxed tolerance for face recognition. Additionally, the performance
                              of the proposed AAS system was compared with the previous study [44] which adopted
                            Dlib HOG and Dlib CNN for face detection, deep residual networks (ResNets) for feature
                              extraction, k-nearest neighbors (KNN) classiﬁer for face recognition in the same video
                             (Figure 11). The pervious study [44] obtained 99 % accuracy. Only a few images were not
                             able to be used to detect and recognize all the four students.

                                   4. Discussion

                                This study was a pilot study because we tested the performance of an AAS system in
                            the laboratory rather than in the classroom. The study proposed a real-time AAS system
                            schematic. Data serialization converted data objects (record images) present in complex
                           data structures into a byte stream for storage, transfer, and distribution purposes on a
                             physical device, which is a good tool for creating a dataset in SQLite. The results shown in
                           Figure 8 reveal the adaptive tolerance for improving the performance of face recognition
                           using Euclidean distance. In addition, Dlib CNN can be said to have a better performance
                               in terms of detecting faces than Dlib HOG. Finally, this study tested a real-time AAS system
                              in a laboratory setting, and the results shown in Section 3.4 indicate that the system was
                             able to detect all of the students and could be registered in the cloud server automatically. In
                            order to verify the performance of a real-time AAS system, we will apply to the Institutional
                        Review Board (IRB) and test the AAS system in a classroom setting in our future work. In
                              addition, this study adopted Euclidean distance with adaptive tolerance to face recognition.
                             Future, the SVM and a more powerful classify method (CNN) will be adopted to compare
                                      its performance and efﬁcacy to related face recognition methods.

                                   5. Conclusions

                                  In this study, we applied a combination of a number of common methods and libraries
                              in order to develop an AAS system. In addition, we used our proposed data serialization
                       and adaptive tolerance for Euclidean-distance methods to optimize the performance of
                                this AAS. Data serialization was utilized in order to support the storing of facial features
                            via SQLite. The calculation of adaptive (rather than ﬁxed) tolerance was shown here
                              to improve the performance of Euclidian-distance-based facial recognition. The results
                            yielded by this study demonstrate that the proposed AAS can recognize multiple faces and
                           so facilitate the automatic marking of attendance. Our proposed AAS would mean, in the
                           classroom situation, that students would not be able to skip classes without the knowledge
                              of their teachers.
                         Our development of this AI model and these techniques supports improvements in
                            the design and application of facial recognition. However, the AAS implemented in this
                          study also has some shortcomings which should be addressed—viz:
                        When the light levels in the classroom are low, this can mean that the proposed system
                           manifests low accuracy in terms of face detection and recognition. In the future, we will
                           explore methods by which the face detector system can be adjusted to work with low
                                light levels.

title: LaED: a novel lightweight, edge-aware and explainable deep learning model for privacy-preserving facial attendance tracking in resource-constrained educational environments

pages.text:
www.nature.com/scientificreports



    OPEN LaED: a novel lightweight, edge-
        aware and explainable deep
          learning model for privacy-
          preserving facial attendance
          tracking in resource-constrained
          educational environments
                         Esther Omolara Abiodun1, Oludare Isaac Abiodun1, Moatsum Alawida2,
                     Bayan Abu Shawar3 & Abid Mehmood2

                               Facial recognition is increasingly adopted for automated classroom attendance; however, real-world
                        deployment in schools remains constrained by privacy risks, ethical obligations, demographic bias,
                           spoofing threats, and limited computational resources. Recent incidents involving Microsoft Teams
                                in New South Wales in 2025 and Chelmer Valley High School in the United Kingdom show how poorly
                         governed systems violate student rights and regulatory compliance. Despite growing adoption, many
                              existing attendance systems focus narrowly on recognition accuracy or efficiency, while overlooking
                          spoof resistance, open-set identity handling, fairness mitigation, auditability, and privacy protection.
                            This paper presents LaED, a lightweight, edge-aware, and explainable deep learning framework for
                             privacy-preserving classroom attendance in resource-constrained educational environments. The
                        framework combines multimodal spoof detection, open-set facial recognition, and fairness-aware
                            representation learning within a unified edge-based design. Spoofing attacks, including replay and
                          deepfake attempts, are mitigated through the fusion of physiological and temporal facial cues,
                           while unknown identities are explicitly rejected to reduce proxy attendance. To support responsible
                         deployment, LaED incorporates federated learning with differential privacy, ensuring that biometric
                          data remain local to schools while enabling accountable model updates. Experimental evaluation
                       on CASIA-FASD, CelebA-Spoof, DFDC, FairFace, and a consent-driven classroom dataset shows that
                      LaED achieves over 97.8% recognition accuracy, APCER and BPCER values below 2%, demographic
                              fairness gaps under 2%, and inference latency below 150 milliseconds on edge hardware. Additional
                              tests confirm reliable operation under realistic classroom conditions. These results demonstrate
                            that regulation-aligned and trustworthy facial attendance is feasible on low-cost devices, offering a
                               practical pathway for responsible biometric AI in education.

                       Keywords  Privacy-preserving facial recognition, Classroom attendance tracking, Lightweight deep learning,
                             Federated learning with differential privacy, Fairness and explainability in AI, Edge intelligence, Green AI

                                 Facial recognition technologies have rapidly gained traction for automating administrative tasks across diverse
                            domains, including law enforcement, border control, healthcare, and education1–3. In classroom contexts,
                           automated attendance systems are promoted as a means to reduce manual errors, save instructional time, and
                              enable real-time reporting for administrators. These perceived advantages have driven experimentation with face-
                              recognition-based attendance platforms in universities, secondary schools, and corporate training programs. As
                             education systems become increasingly digitized and resource constrained, particularly in developing regions,
                               lightweight and real-time solutions are often favored for their efficiency and potential scalability4.
                                 Despite these benefits, the deployment of facial recognition systems in classrooms has raised significant
                            concerns related to privacy, legality, fairness, and accountability. This scrutiny has intensified following several
                               global incidents5,6. Recent incidents, including unauthorized biometric data collection associated with Microsoft
                         Teams in New South Wales in 2025 and regulatory action against Chelmer Valley High School in the United
                         Kingdom, demonstrate how poorly governed systems can violate student rights and fail to meet regulatory
                               compliance7–10. These cases highlight the sensitivity of biometric technologies in educational environments,
                          where users are often minors, regulatory requirements are stringent, and institutional capacity for oversight may
                           be limited. Consequently, classroom attendance systems must satisfy not only performance requirements but
                                also ethical and legal expectations.
                              Although prior research has explored automated attendance using facial recognition, several practical
                                 limitations remain unresolved. Existing systems typically emphasize recognition accuracy, tracking stability, or
                             computational efficiency, while addressing spoof resistance, open-set identity handling, demographic fairness,
                                   auditability, and privacy preservation only in isolation1,2,11–13. Many approaches further rely on assumptions
                                 that do not hold in real classrooms, such as cooperative subjects, static capture conditions, closed-set identities,
                             or centralized processing pipelines. As a result, these systems remain vulnerable to proxy attendance, spoofing
                                  attacks, privacy leakage, and biased outcomes when deployed in realistic educational settings.
                                In this paper, we present LaED, a lightweight, edge-aware, and explainable deep learning framework designed
                                 for privacy-preserving classroom attendance tracking in resource-constrained environments. The framework is
                             motivated by real-world classroom conditions and education-specific biometric threat models, with the aim of
                              enabling robust attendance verification while supporting fairness, transparency, and lawful data governance.
                                 This work makes the following algorithmic contributions:

                                    1.  Fairness-Aware Embedding Regularization: We propose a fairness-aware loss that constrains subgroup em­
                              bedding centroids across age, gender, and skin tone to remain aligned with the global latent space during
                                     training, reducing demographic performance gaps at the representation level.

                      Related studies
                            Research on facial-recognition-based attendance systems has evolved along two complementary dimensions. The
                                         first concerns system-level design choices, including tracking-based pipelines, lightweight and liveness-enabled
                                 solutions, and privacy-aware biometric frameworks. The second focuses on the deep learning architectures used
                                 for facial feature extraction and recognition, ranging from classical convolutional models to transfer learning
                         and transformer-based approaches. While both strands provide valuable insights, their limitations constrain
                           deployment in real classroom environments. The following subsections review these themes and identify
                             unresolved challenges relevant to educational settings.

                         Tracking-oriented approaches
                             Tracking-based methods aim to improve recognition stability by maintaining identity continuity across
                              consecutive frames. Bugingo et al.1 demonstrated that real-time tracking reduces identity-switch errors in
                          dynamic classroom settings, with similar benefits reported in surveillance and workplace analytics14,15. However,
                          most tracking pipelines focus primarily on temporal consistency and do not defend against modern presentation
                                 attacks such as replayed videos or deepfakes16. In addition, privacy-preserving safeguards are typically absent,
                               leaving continuous video streams vulnerable to misuse. Consequently, tracking alone is insufficient for secure
                         and compliant classroom deployment.

                        Lightweight and liveness-based solutions
                  A second line of research emphasizes real-time attendance on low-cost or edge hardware. Surantha and
                               Sugijakko2, Nguyen et al.17, and Al-Waisy et al.18 showed that lightweight CNNs can support efficient classroom
                            deployment. Despite these advantages, many lightweight systems rely on simple liveness cues such as eye
                              blinking or texture analysis, which are vulnerable to three-dimensional masks and deepfake attacks19. Open-
                                   set recognition and demographic fairness controls are also rarely addressed, exposing such systems to proxy
                             attendance and subgroup performance disparities20.

                         Privacy and trust-oriented biometrics
                         Beyond recognition accuracy, recent studies have explored privacy-aware biometric frameworks. Federated
                               learning enables local model training without sharing raw facial images21, while differential privacy mitigates
                              the risk of reconstructing biometric features from model updates22. Tamper-evident audit logs and blockchain-
                            based mechanisms have been proposed to enhance accountability23,24. Although promising, these techniques are
                          seldom integrated into classroom attendance systems and are often evaluated independently of spoof detection,
                                 fairness mitigation, or operational constraints. Real-world incidents, including unauthorized biometric data
                                 collection in New South Wales and regulatory action in the United Kingdom, highlight the risks of deploying
                                    facial recognition without comprehensive governance.

                    Deep learning architectures for facial recognition
                          The effectiveness of attendance systems is also shaped by the underlying model architectures. Classical CNNs
                            such as VGG-Face, ResNet, and MobileNet provide efficient feature extraction but are sensitive to occlusion,
                                 lighting variation, and sophisticated presentation attacks25,26. Transfer learning approaches, including FaceNet
                         and ArcFace, improve recognition accuracy through discriminative embeddings27,28, while MagFace and
                          AdaFace further enhance robustness by linking embedding quality to image characteristics29,30. However, these
                          models often rely on heavy pretrained backbones and closed-set assumptions, limiting their suitability for edge
                           deployment and safe handling of unknown identities. Transformer-based models such as MobileViT, Swin
                              Transformer, and Tiny-ViT improve global context modeling and robustness under real-world variations31,32,
                                yet they rarely integrate liveness detection, fairness calibration, or privacy-preserving training.

                       Comparative analysis of CNN, transfer learning and transformer methods
                     CNN, transfer learning, and transformer architectures each contribute distinct strengths to facial recognition
                               systems. CNNs offer computational efficiency but struggle with global context and spoof resistance. Transfer

                         work on explainable AI and privacy-preserving biometrics, including Grad-CAM, attention rollout, federated
                                learning, and differential privacy, has improved transparency and accountability33–36, but these techniques are
                                  typically applied in isolation rather than within integrated attendance systems.

                   Summary and research gap
                               Existing studies advance facial-recognition-based attendance through improvements in tracking  stability,
                             computational efficiency, recognition accuracy, or privacy protection. However, these advances are fragmented
                               across system-level designs and architectural choices as detailed in Fig. 1. Most existing approaches do not
                              simultaneously address spoof resistance, open-set identity handling, demographic fairness, explainability,
                              privacy preservation, and auditability under realistic classroom conditions. This fragmentation, together with
                         documented regulatory failures and ethical concerns, highlights a persistent gap in the literature and motivates
                              the need for integrated frameworks suitable for trustworthy deployment in educational environments.

                   System architecture of LaED
                      LaED is organized as a three-layer architecture consisting of a Perception Layer, an Identity Layer, and a Trust
                                Layer. Each layer performs a distinct functional role in the attendance pipeline, and together they form an edge-
                              deployable system suitable for classroom environments. The architecture is designed so that input validation,
                                 identity recognition, and governance functions are handled sequentially, with clearly defined data flows between
                                    layers.

                         Perception layer
                          The Perception Layer processes raw visual input captured from classroom cameras and determines whether the
                              input is suitable for identity recognition. Its primary function is to validate incoming facial data and remove
                            manipulated or low-quality inputs before further processing.

                           rPPG-based liveness detection
                         Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) is applied to extract subtle skin color variations associated with blood
                                  flow. These physiological signals are computed in parallel with face detection and are used to distinguish live
                                subjects from static images, replayed videos, or synthetically generated faces.

                            Deepfake and replay detection
                          The Perception Layer includes convolutional  filters trained to detect temporal and texture-level artifacts
                        commonly observed in replay attacks and deepfake content, such as abnormal blinking patterns, inconsistent
                                   reflections, and spatial distortions. Inputs flagged as manipulated are discarded at this stage.

                              Noise reduction and preprocessing
                              Validated facial inputs are normalized, compressed, and denoised to reduce illumination variation and
                           background interference. This step ensures that only standardized and computationally efficient representations
                                are forwarded to the Identity Layer.

                           Identity Layer
                          The Identity Layer performs facial representation learning, identity matching, and decision control. It receives
                                validated facial inputs from the Perception Layer and outputs identity decisions together with confidence and
                                fairness-adjusted scores.

                               Lightweight transformer backbone
                  A Tiny Vision Transformer (Tiny-ViT) serves as the feature extraction backbone. The model uses self-attention
                                to emphasize salient facial regions while suppressing irrelevant background information. Attention-based and
                                multi-scale fusion strategies similar to those reported in recent literature have been shown to improve robustness
                           under real-world variation37.

                             Open-set recognition
                                 Identity matching is performed using an open-set recognition mechanism. Instead of enforcing closed-set
                                    classification, the system applies confidence-based thresholding derived from embedding similarity. Inputs that
                         do not meet acceptance criteria are labeled as unknown and excluded from attendance records.

                                Fairness calibration
                          The Identity Layer incorporates fairness-aware calibration during training and update cycles. Embedding
                                distributions are periodically adjusted to reduce performance disparities across demographic subgroups, using
                               fairness-aware loss constraints applied during federated updates.

                          Trust layer
                          The Trust Layer governs how identity decisions are stored, updated, and audited. It ensures that attendance
                              records are managed in a privacy-preserving and accountable manner.

                              Federated learning with differential privacy
                         Model updates are trained locally on edge devices and aggregated using a federated learning protocol. Differential
                              privacy noise is applied to model updates prior to aggregation, limiting the risk of reconstructing biometric
                             information from transmitted parameters.

                             Tamper-evident audit logs
                          Each attendance decision is recorded in a tamper-evident audit log constructed using cryptographic hash
                               chaining. These logs enable post hoc verification of attendance records by authorized parties.

                            Consent and compliance management
                          The Trust Layer maintains consent records, enforces data retention policies, and supports automated deletion of
                              expired biometric data. These mechanisms regulate access to attendance records in accordance with applicable
                              data protection requirements.

                         Integrated workflow
                          The three layers operate sequentially as an integrated workflow. Facial inputs are first validated by the Perception
                                Layer, then processed by the Identity Layer for recognition and decision control, and finally recorded and
                           governed by the Trust Layer. This separation of responsibilities allows each layer to operate independently while
                             supporting a coherent end-to-end attendance pipeline. Figure 2 illustrates the three-layer architecture and the
                              flow of data across the system.
                            The LaED framework consists of three interconnected layers: the Perception Layer for input validation
                            through rPPG-based liveness detection, deepfake screening, and preprocessing; the Identity Layer for facial
                               representation learning, open-set recognition, and fairness calibration; and the Trust Layer for federated learning
                             with differential privacy, tamper-evident audit logging, and consent management. Together, these layers support
                          an edge-deployable attendance system with clear separation between sensing, decision-making, and governance.

                      Spoof and deepfake detection
                      LaED implements a multi-stream mechanism for detecting presentation attacks and synthetic facial inputs. Two
                          complementary feature streams are used: physiological signal analysis and temporal artifact detection.
                           Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) is applied to short facial video sequences to extract skin color
                                variations associated with blood flow. These signals are computed from temporally aligned skin-region pixels
                         and summarized using frequency-domain and consistency measures. rPPG extraction operates in parallel with
                                face detection and does not introduce additional inference latency.
                                In parallel, a lightweight deepfake detection module based on a Tiny Vision Transformer is trained using
                                selected samples from the DFDC dataset. The detector focuses on temporal inconsistencies such as abnormal
                              blinking patterns, lip-motion irregularities, and local texture artifacts. Outputs from the rPPG and deepfake
                             streams are fused to determine whether an input is bona fide. Only validated inputs are forwarded to the
                              recognition stage. This design addresses spoofing vulnerabilities reported in tracking-based systems1 and
                                 limitations of basic liveness checks used in portable attendance solutions2.

                        Lightweight recognition with open-set thresholding
                                 Identity recognition is performed using a compact Tiny Vision Transformer backbone optimized for edge
                            deployment. Facial embeddings are extracted from normalized input frames and encoded into a low-dimensional
                                  latent space. The self-attention mechanism enables efficient modeling of global facial structure while maintaining
                             a small parameter footprint. Similar attention-based feature fusion strategies have demonstrated improved
                              robustness in recent studies37.
                         LaED employs an open-set recognition strategy based on cosine similarity. Instead of enforcing closed-set
                                    classification, the system applies a confidence threshold derived from the statistical distribution of embeddings.
                              Inputs that fall outside the acceptance boundary are labeled as unknown and excluded from attendance records.
                              This mechanism prevents forced classification of unregistered individuals and supports dynamic classroom
                             environments.

                          Privacy-preserving federated learning
                         Model training and updates are conducted using a federated learning protocol. Each classroom node performs
                                  local training on encrypted datasets, and raw facial images or embeddings are not transmitted. Only gradient
                             updates are shared with the aggregation server. To mitigate reconstruction risks, differential privacy noise is
                          added to gradients prior to transmission38.
                                Federated aggregation is implemented using compressed gradient exchange and adaptive communication
                           rounds to accommodate bandwidth constraints. This configuration enables distributed learning on resource-
                               limited devices while preserving data locality. Details of large-scale federated simulations and hierarchical
                              aggregation are provided in Appendix 2.

                          Fairness calibration
                               Fairness calibration is incorporated directly into the training objective. During evaluation, predictions are
                              disaggregated by age, gender, and skin tone to monitor subgroup performance. A fairness-aware regularization
                           term constrains subgroup embedding centroids to remain aligned with the global latent space.

                       Implementation and training setup
                              This subsection details implementation settings to support reproducibility and deployment transparency.

                          Module interaction and conflict resolution streams
                                 Identity embeddings, rPPG liveness scores, and deepfake-artifact confidence values are calibrated to a common
                          0–1 scale. Decision-level fusion applies rule-guided conflict resolution. If liveness or deepfake confidence
                                       falls below safety thresholds, the sample is rejected regardless of identity similarity. Ambiguous cases result in
                              deferred re-capture rather than forced classification.

                          Data preprocessing
                             Faces are detected using MTCNN and aligned via similarity transforms. Inputs are normalized to 112 × 112 pixels
                         and enhanced using CLAHE. Training augmentations include horizontal flipping, Gaussian blur, brightness
                         and contrast jitter, and random occlusion. rPPG signals are extracted using a 0.7–4.0 Hz bandpass filter and
                          smoothed with a five-frame window.

                          Model architecture
                      LaED uses a Tiny-ViT with 12 transformer blocks, four attention heads per block, a 256-dimensional embedding,
                         and approximately 6.8 million parameters. Positional encoding and residual connections stabilize training and
                              preserve spatial structure.

                               Training procedure
                              Training uses Adam optimization with a learning rate of 1e-4, batch size 32, 40 epochs, and early stopping.
                             Federated learning is implemented using FedAvg with five clients and aggregation every two epochs. Differential
                              privacy is applied using Opacus with noise multiplier σ = 0.75 and clipping norm C = 1.0, yielding ε ≈ 8.2 at
                                    δ = 10⁻⁵.

                               Feature extraction and fusion
                            Three feature streams are extracted: identity embeddings, rPPG-based physiological features, and deepfake-
                                    artifact features. Decision-level fusion combines scores as.
                                    S = 0.55Sid+0.25SrPPG+0.20Sdf.
                                   Safety overrides are applied when spoof indicators dominate.

                          Hardware and software environment
                            Experiments were conducted on NVIDIA Jetson Nano and Raspberry Pi 4 devices, with pretraining on an RTX
                           2080 Ti workstation. The software stack includes Ubuntu 20.04, PyTorch 2.1, CUDA 11.4, TensorRT 8.5, and
                           Opacus. Figure 3 presents a high-level overview of the complete processing workflow.
                            The figure illustrates the end-to-end pipeline, including preprocessing, Tiny-ViT feature extraction, parallel
                                 liveness and deepfake analysis, decision-level fusion, and attendance verification.

                         Evaluation metrics
                          The performance of LaED was measured using a wide range of indicators. Accuracy alone was not considered
                                    sufficient, since a system that is highly accurate in one condition but fails under attack or discriminates across
                            groups cannot be considered reliable. Instead, the evaluation relied on multiple dimensions.
                                Recognition quality was measured using accuracy, precision, recall, and the F1-score. To evaluate resilience
                                against spoofing attacks, we relied on the two metrics standard in presentation attack detection: the Attack
                               Presentation Classification Error Rate (APCER) and the Bona Fide Presentation Classification Error Rate
                          (BPCER). These allow a precise distinction between the cost of false acceptances and false rejections. For the
                             deepfake detection module, we reported Equal Error Rate (EER) and ROC-AUC, which capture the balance
                           between sensitivity and specificity.
                               Latency and efficiency were evaluated in terms of the average inference time per frame, measured in
                                milliseconds, and memory footprint in megabytes. To ensure that the model could be realistically deployed,
                               these values were collected not only on standard laptops but also on low-power devices such as Raspberry Pi
                         and Jetson Nano. In addition, energy consumption per frame was calculated to reflect battery requirements in
                               portable contexts. Fairness was measured as the maximum subgroup performance gap across gender, racial,
                         and age categories in the FairFace dataset. A fairness gap above 5% was considered unacceptable, and LaED’s
                                 calibration was tested against this threshold.
                                       Finally, scalability indicators such as communication cost in federated training and throughput in multi-user
                                sessions were measured. These indicators were particularly important to demonstrate that LaED can be deployed
                               across campuses or across institutions without creating bottlenecks.

                         Ablation studies
                             Ablation experiments were conducted to evaluate the contribution of individual components. Disabling rPPG-
                            based liveness detection increased vulnerability to replay and photo attacks. Removing deepfake detection
                            reduced robustness to synthetic manipulations. Excluding open-set recognition resulted in false acceptances of
                               unregistered individuals. Omitting fairness calibration increased subgroup error disparities. Replacing federated
                               learning with centralized training eliminated privacy guarantees. These results demonstrate the complementary
                                 role of each module.

                     Deployment environment
                          The deployment of LaED was tested across several hardware platforms to simulate the variety of environments
                          where an attendance system might be expected to operate. On the low end, experiments were run on Raspberry
                               Pi 4 devices with eight gigabytes of RAM. These tests demonstrated whether the system could function in
                              schools with minimal computing resources. At the mid-tier level, we used NVIDIA Jetson Nano devices, which
                                   offer GPU acceleration but remain within the power and cost limits of edge devices commonly used in IoT
                             networks. For comparison, standard laptops with Intel i5 processors and 16 gigabytes of RAM were used to
                           measure performance under typical administrative setups.
                                Federated training was simulated across five classroom nodes using a Kubernetes cluster. Each node performed
                                  local training on a separate partition of the dataset, and the server aggregated the updates asynchronously. To
                                    reflect realistic conditions, communication bandwidth was throttled during some experiments, allowing us to
                           measure resilience under unstable networks. Differential privacy libraries were integrated into the PyTorch 2.1
                          framework to guarantee that individual contributions were obfuscated before aggregation. TensorRT acceleration
                          was employed for inference on the edge devices, ensuring low latency.
                           By conducting experiments across this spectrum of environments, the study demonstrates that LaED is not
                             confined to laboratory conditions. It can operate within the limitations of resource-constrained schools while
                             maintaining consistency with the requirements of privacy regulations and ethical expectations.

                       Results and comparative analysis
                              This section provides an extensive evaluation of the LaED framework across recognition accuracy, spoof and
                             deepfake resistance, robustness to adversarial perturbations, cross-domain generalization, computational
                                    efficiency, fairness, federated learning performance, and usability. The goal is to determine whether LaED
                             meaningfully improves on existing lightweight and tracking-based approaches, and whether the gains are

                          Adversarial robustness tests
                         To complement spoofing and deepfake evaluations, we conducted preliminary adversarial robustness tests using
                              gradient-based attacks: Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM, ε = 0.01–0.05) and Projected Gradient Descent
                         (PGD, 10 steps, ε = 0.03). LaED maintained 83.5% accuracy under FGSM (ε = 0.01) and 78.2% under PGD
                                     (ε = 0.03), outperforming a ResNet baseline which dropped to 62.4% and 55.8% respectively. While accuracy
                           degraded under stronger perturbations (PGD ε = 0.05 → 68.1%), the results indicate that LaED exhibits resilience
                                against moderate adaptive adversarial attacks, reinforcing its suitability for high-stakes and real-time educational
                             environments. Table 5 provides the breakdown of results.
                               Transformer-based architectures appear more resilient to adversarial noise because self-attention layers
                                 distribute feature importance across spatial regions. CNNs rely more heavily on localized edge and texture cues,
                             so small pixel-level perturbations cause sharper degradation in the ResNet baseline.

                          Fairness and demographic robustness
                            Ensuring equitable performance across demographic groups is a critical requirement for biometric-based
                             attendance and identification systems, particularly in educational environments characterized by diverse age,

                      One of the strongest criticisms of facial recognition in education has been the lack of informed consent. High-
                                   profile cases, such as the unauthorized biometric data collection by Microsoft Teams in New South Wales in
                        March 2025, have highlighted how easily privacy rights can be violated when consent protocols are not respected.
                             In another case, Chelmer Valley High School in the United Kingdom faced reprimand after deploying a face-

                           even well-intentioned deployments can cross legal boundaries if they neglect privacy safeguards.
                         LaED incorporates privacy-preserving mechanisms directly into its design. By using federated learning,
                              student data never leaves the local classroom environment. The model updates, not the images, are aggregated at
                              the global level, ensuring that personal biometric data remains confined. Furthermore, the inclusion of consent
                             tokens within the verifiable logging system creates a record that each student’s data use has been authorized. In
                                   this way, LaED transforms privacy from an afterthought into a foundational component of system design.

                          Fairness and equity
                                Ethical concerns also extend beyond privacy into the question of fairness. Face recognition models have
                                   historically been prone to demographic  bias, disproportionately misclassifying students from minority
                            backgrounds. If left unaddressed, these disparities can reinforce existing inequalities and undermine trust in the
                               technology. Our evaluation demonstrated that without calibration, subgroup performance gaps exceeded 9%, a
                                   level that could produce unequal educational outcomes.
                           By embedding fairness calibration into every training cycle, LaED ensures that subgroup performance
                                 differences  are minimized and monitored.  Importantly,  the  fairness  process  is  transparent,  allowing
                              administrators to view disaggregated results rather than only aggregate accuracy. This design choice responds to
                           growing calls from policymakers and advocacy groups who argue that algorithmic systems should be auditable
                                 for equity. The framework therefore does not only enhance technical reliability but also safeguards the principle
                                of equal treatment.

                         Synthetic data justification
                               Synthetic augmentation played both an ethical and technical role. Ethically, it reduced reliance on collecting
                                  sensitive biometric data from children, respecting privacy norms. Technically, it improved demographic balance:
                              the inclusion of StyleGAN3 faces reduced the accuracy gap between lighter and darker skin tones from 7.4%
                                to 2.1%. This aligns with recent works leveraging GANs for fairness-aware augmentation43–46. While concerns
                            about “GAN artifacts” are valid, careful curation and exclusion of low-quality generations minimized risks.
                            Hence, synthetic data served as both a fairness equalizer and a privacy-preserving strategy, integral to LaED’s
                             design philosophy.

                        Legal and regulatory compliance
                             Regulatory frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation in Europe and the Family Educational
                              Rights and Privacy Act in the United States impose strict requirements on the handling of student data.
                          Compliance with these regulations is not optional; institutions that fail to meet standards risk legal penalties and
                               reputational harm. Baseline systems did not include compliance mechanisms and would likely face challenges
                                             if deployed at scale.
                         LaED takes a proactive stance by embedding compliance markers into its verifiable logs. Each attendance
                             record is tied to a consent statement, and all logs are tamper-evident, making  it possible to demonstrate
                            adherence to regulations during audits. Beyond technical compliance, this transparency creates a climate of
                                 accountability, giving stakeholders confidence that the system can withstand legal and regulatory examination.
                    A further ethical consideration involves the use of synthetic data for fairness calibration. While synthetic
                            augmentation helps reduce demographic imbalance without collecting additional biometric data from students,
                                             it also introduces potential risks if the generative model embeds biased or unrealistic facial characteristics. To
                               mitigate this, all StyleGAN3-generated faces were screened for visual artifacts, over-representation of particular
                           phenotype traits, and distributional skew. Synthetic samples were used strictly as non-identifiable fairness-
                              balancing inputs and were never mixed with real student embeddings in the attendance database. Moreover,
                           subgroup performance was evaluated on real faces only, ensuring that fairness gains observed in LaED are
                            not artefacts of synthetic data alone. These safeguards help ensure that synthetic faces improve equity without
                              introducing new ethical vulnerabilities or reinforcing hidden biases in the model.
                              Deploying facial recognition in education involves navigating a wide range of regulatory, cultural and
                                  institutional environments. Some regions operate under comprehensive child-data governance frameworks such
                                as GDPR or FERPA, while others have fragmented or minimal oversight. This variability affects how schools
                                 interpret consent, how they store biometric data and how violations are investigated or penalized. LaED’s privacy-
                              preserving architecture was designed to accommodate these differences by keeping all biometric processing on
                                  local devices, providing cryptographically verifiable logs and supporting granular consent tracking. Even so,
                                technical safeguards cannot fully compensate for weak institutional governance. Schools with limited digital
                                   literacy or inconsistent enforcement practices may struggle to maintain robust access control, incident handling
                         and parental communication procedures. These challenges highlight that LaED can help reduce risk but must
                              operate within a broader ecosystem of policy, training and regulatory accountability. Scaling the system across
                                diverse jurisdictions will require adaptation to local norms, integration with region-specific legal requirements
                         and ongoing monitoring to ensure that privacy commitments are upheld in practice.
                                      Scalability in educational environments extends beyond initial deployment on low-power devices. Sustaining
                           performance over time requires mechanisms that can adapt to demographic changes, evolving attack strategies,
                         and hardware degradation. New deepfake generation techniques, mask materials, or adversarial manipulation
                          methods may emerge, and demographic composition in classrooms may shift as student cohorts change. LaED
                              addresses part of this challenge through its modular design, which allows periodic recalibration of open-set
                                thresholds, incremental federated re-training without transferring raw data, and continuous monitoring of
                           subgroup performance. These capabilities help maintain fairness, privacy and robustness as conditions evolve.
                               Nevertheless, long-term sustainability also depends on institutional practices such as scheduled model audits,

                              Regulatory mapping
                         To strengthen the legal and ethical grounding of LaED, we explicitly map relevant regulatory requirements
                                to concrete system features. Table 14 illustrates how LaED operationalizes obligations under GDPR, FERPA,
                         and UNICEF child protection guidelines. This mapping moves beyond abstract claims by demonstrating direct

                            minimization (Art. 5(1)(c)) is addressed through on-device embeddings and federated learning, which prevent
                              the transfer of raw biometric data. Similarly, the right to erasure (Art. 17) is implemented via consent tokens
                         and a retention manager that allow secure deletion of attendance records within institutionally defined retention
